prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and for the design of long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonists that made it a therapy for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I still place B006 alone. All six of us put it first or second, nobody raises a maturity objection, and the evidence chain is complete and independently confirmed: proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, human GLP-1 physiology and extra-pancreatic actions, then durable agonists with replicated benefit in diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. Holst and Drucker are the secure physiological core. I keep Knudsen as the third name because the physiology became a medicine only when a peptide with a half-life of minutes was turned into a once-weekly drug through acylation and albumin binding. That is a scientific achievement with a named, documented author, not only industrial output. The citation I propose says both things, discovery of the physiology and design of the long-acting agonists, so that the choice of the third name is explicit and not made by default, which is the chair's request.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is the third seat. Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36/37) peptide is a fundamental early step, and Habener, who is outside the credited list, worked in the same period. My preferred trio omits her, and four colleagues who favor a discovery-only citation could fairly say that I am rewarding development ahead of identification. I also cannot settle the priority record from the supplied material, so my preference for Knudsen rests partly on an attribution that is less disputed, not on a proven ranking of scientific importance. Crediting an industry scientist is unusual for this prize and a reader may see it as a break with the tradition of rewarding discovery.

responses.point: Linnarsson accepts Knudsen over Mojsov only if Mojsov's priority cannot be defended, and says development has usually been left to the Lasker clinical awards while the prize is for discovery.
responses.response: I think the Lasker point is partly right but does not decide this. The Nobel record includes awards where the step that made a mechanism usable was credited, for example recombinant and monoclonal technologies and, more recently, mRNA modification that enabled vaccines. So development is not excluded in principle. Your conditional is also fair, and I would apply it symmetrically: if the committee cannot defend Mojsov's priority from documents, Knudsen is the natural third name, and if it can, the choice is a real decision about what the citation rewards. I am still not persuaded that the record is clear enough for the first reading. I have not moved on the name, but I accept that the dispute turns on the citation and I am not treating it as settled by counting votes.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that the citation is strongest for how GLP-1 works as a hormone and its active form, that analogue engineering is a later, partly proprietary step with a large team behind it, and that Mojsov's identification made the physiology interpretable.
responses.response: The large-team point is the part of your argument I weigh most, because the Nobel rules need a specific person and Knudsen's group is a real concern. Here I think the record helps me: the albumin-binding acylation concept behind liraglutide and semaglutide is associated with a specific line of work that she led, which is more traceable than the priority among Mojsov, Habener and others. I also agree that identification of the active form made interpretation possible. We disagree on weighing, not on the facts. If we can agree that the citation names the physiology and the long-acting agonists, I think the committee has the more honest position, whichever third name it ends on.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would favor Knudsen only if the committee decides explicitly that the citation is for the therapy, and wants Mojsov's priority resolved before choosing. She also asks that industry credit not be settled implicitly through the third name.
responses.response: I accept that framing and I think my proposal meets it: I am deciding explicitly that the citation should name both physiology and development, and I am saying so in the text, not hiding it in the name list. On industry credit, my view is that it is a consequence of who held the decisive contribution and not a principle that a company programme deserves a prize. Where you and I differ is the order of evidence: you want priority resolved before moving to Knudsen, and I would resolve it by choosing the attribution that does not depend on the dispute. If the committee prefers your sequence and finds Mojsov defensible, I would vote for that configuration without reservation about Drucker and Holst.

responses.point: El-Manira says that if the priority record proves unclear, Drucker, Holst and Knudsen becomes the safer choice, and that replacing Mojsov shifts the prize from discovery to development while basic-science credit is argued.
responses.response: We are close. You and I both say that the unresolved priority record is what decides the third seat, and neither of us has verified it from primary documents. The difference is the default if it stays unresolved: you keep Mojsov until it proves unclear, and I start from the more settled attribution. Since no member can settle it from the supplied material, I think the safer course for the committee is the one that does not rest on a contested claim, and your own statement that you would not block Drucker, Holst and Knudsen supports that. I would not block Mojsov either.

responses.point: The chair asks whether Rosenberg and early originators outside the credited names of B019 can be handled in a citation, and whether attribution is the main reason B019 ranks below B006, and sets out a second-part question around B001, B019 and B016.
responses.response: For B019 I rank it second because the clinical proof is strong, but attribution is indeed why it stays an alternative. A citation can name CAR-T therapy but cannot repair the omission of Eshhar, and Rosenberg's work is adoptive cell therapy more broadly. A second part within the three-person cap would also cut the GLP-1 trio to two, which I do not accept. I therefore keep B006 as the sole part. Among the alternatives I now put B016 ahead of B002: Perlmann and you showed that Walter and Mori is the cleanest pair on the list, and my concern about six names in B002 has not been resolved.

uncertainties: Whether the documentary record lets the committee defend Mojsov over Habener and others for the active GLP-1(7-36/37) peptide. I cannot verify it from the supplied material, and my choice of Knudsen depends on it.
Whether the committee should accept an industry scientist as a laureate for the long-acting agonists, or treat a discovery-only citation as the better reading of the prize.
Whether B019 can be fairly credited without Eshhar, and whether B016 will be a stronger candidate in a later year once disease links mature.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific conflict. My profile records no collaboration, training link or institutional tie to Drucker, Holst, Knudsen, Mojsov or any other credited name on the shortlist. I disclose eight co-authored works with Sten Linnarsson and prior joint work with Jonas Frisen, none of which concerns a shortlisted candidate. I am not recusing.
